1.pericope_label: And take thou unto thee Aaron thy brother, and his sons with him, from among the children of Israel, that he may minister unto me in the priest’s office; and thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother for glory and for beauty

schools.summary: Gill reads the opening verb as a summons to be distinguished and separated in the name of the Lord, and notes that the garments are described before the work or the consecration, covering the man entirely against the heathen practice of sacrificing naked. Calvin makes the calling itself the proof of the office’s dignity: no man taketh this honour unto himself, heathen priesthoods were filled by popular election so that ambition alone governed the appointment, and not even Christ would have sufficed to propitiate God had he not undertaken the office by his Father’s decree. Calvin also holds that the ornaments denote the want of what is true and spiritual, concealing Aaron’s faults before representing virtue, and condemns the later sale of the priesthood while insisting the counsel of God remained inviolable through it.

Henry reads Moses’ passing over his own family as character: an instance of the humility of that great man, who was not desirous to engross all the honours to himself and was very well pleased to see his brother invested, with Aaron, who had humbly served as prophet to his younger brother, now advanced, since God will exalt those that abase themselves.

Clarke argues that the same fact is evidence rather than character, since a man acting on his own authority would not have left his own descendants ordinary Levites while settling the nation’s only dignity on his brother’s house, and notes that the priests held no secular power until the Asmoneans. He also turns the phrase for glory and for beauty against the dismal black of his own century’s ministers. Wesley repeats Henry’s judgement and draws the practical reason for a settled priesthood, that those who ministered at the altar had to give themselves wholly to the service.

Ellicott renders the command literally as make to draw near, and observes that the absolutely unique position of Moses as sole intermediary and sole priest was now ending, whether from his original want of faith or from Aaron’s elder birth. He traces the succession through Eleazar and Ithamar to Phinehas and eventually to Eli, and separates the two stated ends of the dress, glory to exalt the priests in the eyes of the nation and beauty to harmonise them with the adorned tabernacle, concluding that beauty is not despised by the Creator. Keil opens the description with the ephod and calls its etymology uncertain.

debates: Whether Moses’ exclusion of his own line proves divine appointment (Clarke) or displays personal humility (Henry).
Whether the holy garments chiefly exalt the priest (Ellicott) or chiefly cover his defect (Calvin).
outliers: Clarke applies the phrase for glory and for beauty polemically to contemporary clerical dress, asking whether black is emblematical of anything good.

3.pericope_label: And thou shalt speak unto all that are wise hearted, whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, that they may make Aaron’s garments to consecrate him; and these are the garments which they shall make; a breastplate, and an ephod, and a robe, and a broidered coat, a mitre, and a girdle

schools.summary: Gill reads wise hearted as knowledge and understanding in mechanic arts, and notes that garments so uncommon required more than ordinary skill, thought and judgment to make exactly; on the materials he adds from the Targum of Jonathan that the makers took nothing out of their own substance but received from Moses what the people had freely offered. Calvin opens his treatment of the dress by warning readers to abandon all subtle speculations and be contented with simplicity, since he could repeat many plausible allegories that would find more favour with some than a sound knowledge of facts.

Clarke turns the clause into a general doctrine of genius: ingenuity in arts and sciences, even the ornamental kind, comes from God, and no man ever acquired such a genius by reading or study, so that what we call natural Moses teaches us to consider divine. He names Napier, Copernicus, Kepler and Newton, appeals to the ploughman whom his God doth instruct to discretion, and twice checks himself with the warning that machinery must help the human hand and not supersede it, since zeal for machinery is filling the land with beggary and the workhouses with paupers. On the list of garments he works philologically, deriving the robe from a root meaning to go up and citing Josephus that it was woven throughout in one piece, giving the broidered coat from Parkhurst as a close strait garment, tracing the mitre to a root meaning to wrap round and connecting it with the eastern turban, and describing the girdle as the sash in which long skirts were tucked up for work or a journey.

Ellicott explains wise hearted as those having the special knowledge to give effectual aid, and notes the Hebrew habit of making the heart the seat of knowledge as no less accurate than our own of making it the seat of the affections. He grants that few passages are more antagonistic to modern thought than God infusing his Spirit to enable men to produce priestly garments, and answers that God is the fountain of all knowledge, that he alone knows what is beneath him, and that dress is not insignificant or Scripture would say less about it. He then arranges the six garments in order, noting that the high priest’s are described through thirty-six verses, that the breastplate stands first as most conspicuous, that the ephod was a jerkin or waistcoat, and that nothing is said of footwear though sandals are probable; the materials he identifies as those of the vail and curtains with gold and precious stones added.

debates: Whether the endowment of the craftsmen is a special infusion for this task (Ellicott, defending the text against modern instinct) or the ordinary divine origin of all artistic genius (Clarke).
outliers: Clarke leaves the verse entirely to argue that mechanisation is impoverishing the labouring class, a social application with no basis in the text.

6.pericope_label: And they shall make the ephod of gold, of blue, and of purple, of scarlet, and fine twined linen, with cunning work: it shall have the two shoulderpieces thereof joined at the two edges thereof; and the curious girdle of the ephod shall be of the same

schools.summary: Gill sets the rabbinic authorities against one another on the ephod’s length — to the loins per Kimchi, to the buttocks per Abarbinel, not to the feet as Jarchi and Maimonides held, since Josephus makes it a cubit — and describes the back and front pieces buttoned with onyx stones at the shoulders, contradicting Josephus again by denying it had sleeves. He describes the shoulder pieces meeting from before and behind, and takes the ephod as a symbol of the human nature of Christ.

Henry calls it the golden ephod for the quantity of gold woven into it, distinguishing it from the plain linen ephods of inferior priests, of Samuel as a child and of David dancing before the ark, and reads it forward to Christ: girt about with a golden girdle in the vision of John, righteousness the girdle of his loins, the government upon his shoulders as Aaron bore the names of Israel there, bearing them before the Lord for a memorial as representative and advocate.

Clarke observes that the word rendered curious girdle signifies merely a kind of diaper or embroidered work and is widely different from the word properly translated girdle, and reports the two consequences drawn from this — that the shoulder connectors were to match the ephod’s texture, or that a distinct girdle of only plain workmanship is meant. Wesley follows Henry’s account of the garment and its application to Christ in the same terms.

Keil argues from the parallel account that the ephod was two pieces joined over the shoulders, against Knobel’s single piece with armholes, reasoning from silence that a garment drawn over the head would have had its head-opening mentioned as the robe’s is, and so endorsing the rabbinical description of two pieces reaching to the hip. On the girdle he traces the word to a root meaning to bind, giving cingulum rather than the Greek version’s weaving. Ellicott corrects the article to two shoulder pieces, holds that the word means device or ornamental work without itself meaning belt while accepting Josephus’ description of a girdle dyed of many hues with gold interwoven, and explains of the same as woven continuously rather than sewn on.

debates: Whether the ephod was two pieces joined at the shoulders (Keil, with the rabbis, against Knobel) or a single garment with armholes.
Whether the curious girdle is a separate belt or simply embroidered work continuous with the ephod (Clarke reports both; Ellicott and Keil settle for a girdle on lexical grounds).
outliers: Gill twice contradicts Josephus, on the ephod’s length and on whether it had sleeves, while Ellicott and Clarke both rely on Josephus for the girdle.

9.pericope_label: And thou shalt take two onyx stones, and grave on them the names of the children of Israel, six of their names on one stone, and the other six names of the rest on the other stone, according to their birth; and Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial

schools.summary: Gill lists the ancient identifications of the stone without settling among them — the name taken from the colour of a man’s nail, beryl in Onkelos, Jonathan and the Syriac, emerald in the Greek, crystal in the Arabic, sardonyx in Josephus with Braunius approving — and places the six eldest names on the right shoulder. Calvin canvasses three readings of memorial, that God may be mindful of Israel, that the priest may remember them, or that they may remember God is reconciled, adopts none, and interprets it as a monument of the mutual agreement; his own emphasis is that engraving the names removed all occasion of envy, since the people would understand that this one man was not separated for private advantage but that in him they were all a kingdom of priests.

Clarke claims that engraving on precious stones reached in antiquity a perfection never since rivalled, particularly among the Greeks, and that the Greeks very likely borrowed the art from the Hebrews since it flourished in Egypt and Palestine first. He derives the word rendered ouches from a root meaning to close or enclose, prefers socket as the proper translation, and states that ouch cannot be traced up to any legitimate authority. On the memorial he flags the anthropomorphism, that speaking after the manner of men God was to be put in mind of the children of Israel whenever the high priest appeared. Wesley describes the settings as hollow places such as are made in gold rings to receive and hold the stones.

Ellicott decides the stone on technical grounds, preferring onyx or the three-layered sardonyx because emeralds could not have been cut by any process then known while onyx served early for signets, and defends the engraving historically from Chaldaean signet cylinders dated to about 2000 B.C., Egyptian signets reaching the twelfth dynasty, and the likelihood that Israelites had worked in Egyptian shops during the servitude. He states the arithmetical difficulty of the twelve names — either Levi was omitted or Joseph replaced Ephraim and Manasseh — traces ouches to old French nouch, a buckle or clasp, on Skeat’s authority, and corrects the memorial to be for the children of Israel rather than to them, reminding God that the priest pleaded in their name. Keil reads according to their generations as by age, following Josephus in dividing elder and younger between the shoulders, notes that the chains were twisted gold thread rather than links, and argues from the shoulder as the seat of office and its insignia that the names there mark the priest as bringing the nation to God.

debates: What the stone was: Gill leaves five ancient identifications standing while Ellicott rules out emerald on the ground that the cutting technology did not exist.
Whether the English word ouches has any traceable derivation: Clarke says it cannot be traced to any legitimate authority; Ellicott derives it from old French nouch on Skeat’s authority.
Whom the memorial is addressed to — God, the priest, or Israel: Calvin lists all three readings and adopts none, while Ellicott and Clarke both make it a memorial before God.
outliers: Ellicott alone confronts the arithmetic of engraving twelve tribal names, and offers two incompatible solutions without choosing.
Clarke’s claim that Greek gem-engraving was borrowed from the Hebrews goes well beyond anything the text supports.

15.pericope_label: And thou shalt make the breastplate of judgment with cunning work; foursquare it shall be being doubled; and thou shalt set in it settings of stones, even four rows of stones; and the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names

schools.summary: Gill makes the title admonitory, a standing reminder that the priest should do justice, have the people’s judgment at heart, and in hard cases ask it of God and faithfully declare it. Working through the stones he keeps meeting interchangeable pairs, citing De Dieu’s rule that whoever renders one stone emerald must render the next carbuncle and vice versa; he derives the ligure from the lynx, or rather from its spots, following Danaeus in identifying it with the star-flecked stellina, notes that the agate was formerly esteemed and that Pyrrhus of Epirus owned one showing the nine Muses and Apollo by nature and not by art, and takes the fourth row to open with a sea-green stone because the word behind it means the sea. He reports and rejects the suggestion that Levi’s name was omitted.

Henry proposes reading the command as give, or add, or deliver to the breastplate the illuminations and perfections, so that no new object need be made; he leaves open whether Levi had a stone, with Ephraim and Manasseh distinct as Jacob said, or had none and the two were one in Joseph; and he insists that the ephod as garment of service and the breastplate as emblem of honour must by no means be separated.

Clarke grounds the title in practice, the priest wearing it to ask counsel and to sit as judge teaching the law and determining controversies, gives the dimensions as a span square when doubled with the Urim and Thummim placed between the folds, and tabulates all twelve stones against the sons in birth order after the Jerusalem Targum and Ainsworth, objecting that Jonathan’s alignment of the four rows with the four quarters of the world could only hold if the thing lay flat. He then withdraws his own confidence, unable to assert that his identifications or his tribal order are what Moses intended, and states that he has omitted the fabulous accounts and the spiritual meanings others find in each stone as puerile, futile, and not a few dangerous. Wesley follows Henry on the count of the tribes.

Ellicott denies that the Hebrew word means breastplate, giving ornament, and derives the epithet of judgment from its containing the Urim and Thummim. He reckons the span at about nine inches, and argues the doubling was structural: Symmachus renders the word a receptacle or bag, and material objects to be put inside would require it, since strength alone would not, Egypt having produced linen corselets able to resist a sword. He notes that the square carries the idea of perfection where twelve gems would otherwise suit an oblong, and insists on twelve stones, neither more nor fewer, each standing for one tribe. Keil observes that the gold borders round the settings not only ornamented the stones but helped fix them more firmly.

debates: Whether the doubling of the fabric was for strength or to form a pouch for the Urim and Thummim (Ellicott argues the latter from Symmachus; Clarke assumes it).
Whether Levi had a stone of his own: Gill rejects the omission, Henry and Wesley leave both arrangements open, Ellicott only insists the count was twelve.
outliers: Clarke ends his long catalogue of the stones by disclaiming it, saying the data do not preclude mistake and that he has deliberately suppressed both the fabulous lore and the spiritual meanings attached to the gems.

22.pericope_label: And thou shalt make upon the breastplate chains at the ends of wreathen work of pure gold; and they shall bind the breastplate by the rings thereof unto the rings of the ephod with a lace of blue, that the breastplate be not loosed from the ephod; and Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart

schools.summary: Gill reports the Targum of Jonathan’s rendering of the chains as of a determined size, exactly alike in length and thickness, or terminable ones with ends rather than circular like a locket, and notes that some make them rope-work twisted like cables. He counts the three pairs of rings as they come, guesses that rings on the shoulder settings received the far ends of the chains, and records an alternative construction of the verb bind as lift up, so that the breastplate would be raised to join the ephod above it. On the last verse he turns representation into a history, the tribes represented in eternity and in time, in Christ’s sufferings, death, burial and resurrection, and now in heaven where they sit together in him.

Ellicott gives the chains as either of equal length or of wreathen work, literally after the manner of ropes, places the first pair of rings on the upper corners with the chains passed through them to the settings of the ephod and the second pair at the extreme edge of the lower corners, and reads the two placements of the names together: the priest wholly identified with the people, bearing them on his shoulders as supporting and wrestling for them and on his heart as loving them, a twofold memorial appealing at once to God’s power and to his mercy. Keil holds that the chain verse simply repeats the earlier command, arguing from their single mention in the account of the work executed and from their being fastened to the same rosettes; he places the remaining rings inward toward the ephod and on the shoulder pieces near the joining, explains the hyacinth threads as holding the breastplate above the girdle without shifting, and glosses the verb behind not loosed as to move away.

debates: Whether the chain verse adds anything or merely repeats the earlier instruction (Keil argues it is a simple repetition).
How to construe the verb rendered bind: Keil takes it mechanically of tying the rings together, while Gill records an alternative sense of lifting the breastplate up to the ephod.
outliers: Ellicott alone reads the shoulder-stones and the breast-stones as a deliberate pair, assigning power to the one placement and mercy to the other.

30.pericope_label: And thou shalt put in the breastplate of judgment the Urim and the Thummim; and they shall be upon Aaron’s heart, when he goeth in before the LORD: and Aaron shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel upon his heart before the LORD continually

schools.summary: Gill reports that interpreters Jewish and Christian alike are at a loss, lists the guesses — the two words themselves written and folded in, the divine name, little images like the teraphim, or a purely divine work — and then follows Josephus in identifying the Urim and Thummim with the twelve stones, arguing from distribution that the stones and the Urim are never mentioned together. Calvin reports the same two options, that they were distinct from the whole work or were the twelve stones, and prefers a third: that the breastplate itself represented light in doctrine and entire uprightness of life, the judgment of the children of Israel being a certain and defined system, an absolutely perfect rule to which they ought to conform.

Clarke states flatly that what these were has never yet been discovered, and numbers his reasons: nowhere described, no direction given for making them, apparently not made on this occasion, so that if man’s work at all they were articles already in use. He cites Rabbi Menachem that they were no artificer’s work but a mystery delivered to Moses from the mouth of God, and reports that the Samaritan text adds a clause absent from the Hebrew, thou shalt make the Urim and the Thummim, which if admitted would mean they were manufactured here like everything else. He takes lights and perfections to signify the information in spiritual things afforded under the law and the holiness it required, notes that no ancient version supposes anything material is meant, and adduces from Diodorus the Egyptian chief judge’s golden chain bearing a jewelled image called Truth, turned toward the party whose cause was just. Wesley calls the Urim and Thummim the high priest’s cabinet council under a theocracy, and records that the oracle was lost in the captivity and never retrieved.

Ellicott argues they were material objects on three grounds — the phrase matches that for putting the two tables into the ark, the article at first mention implies familiar objects, and Philo and Josephus agree on materiality though on nothing else — then eliminates both ancient candidates, since the two sides of the breastplate were not put in after completion and the twelve jewels are distinguished from the Urim in the same passage. He lists the modern suggestions (cut and uncut diamonds, metal slips marked yes and no, lots, teraphim-like images), judges certainty unattainable while inclining to the images, and holds that how the consultation worked admits of no solution. Keil insists the preposition denotes putting one thing into another and never suspending upon, so that against Knobel the Urim were distinct from the breastplate and placed inside it, and holds the thing was called the breastplate of judgment precisely because they were in it.

debates: Whether the Urim and Thummim were the twelve stones themselves (Gill, with Josephus) or objects distinct from them and placed inside the breastplate (Ellicott, Keil).

Whether they were material objects at all: Clarke doubts anything material is designed and cites Rabbi Menachem, while Ellicott argues materiality from grammar, the article, and the ancient witnesses.
Whether the Urim were placed in the breastplate or suspended on it: Keil argues in, against Knobel, noting the Greek version reads upon.
outliers: Clarke reports a Samaritan plus, thou shalt make the Urim and the Thummim, which is absent from the Hebrew and would settle the question of manufacture if accepted.
Ellicott declines the second half of the problem entirely, saying the manner of consultation admits of no solution and referring the curious reader elsewhere.

31.pericope_label: And thou shalt make the robe of the ephod all of blue; and beneath upon the hem of it thou shalt make pomegranates, and bells of gold between them round about: and it shall be upon Aaron to minister: and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD, that he die not

schools.summary: Gill makes the robe longer than the ephod and worn beneath it but of quite different materials, linen only and wholly blue without figures, and presses its seamlessness on Josephus’ authority — not two parts, not sewed at shoulder or side, but one long piece of woven work — drawing the comparison with the seamless coat of Christ as an emblem of a righteousness with nothing of men’s works joined to it; he derives the garment’s name from a word for prevarication because it covers the sins of God’s people. Calvin allegorises the trimming and defends the practice: pomegranates have no smell, yet the type suggested one to the eye, as if God required a savour as well as a sound, and sinners are sweet to God only as covered with the garment of Christ, which procures favour solely by the sound of the Gospel; he quotes Gregory that the priest is worthy of death from whom the voice of preaching is not heard.

Henry describes the robe as sleeveless and drawn on over the head, with side openings for the arms or, per Maimonides, not sewed at the sides at all, and explains the bells as giving notice to the people in the outer court when the priest went in to burn incense, so that they might apply themselves to their devotions at the same time in token of their concurrence with him.

Clarke, following Josephus, makes the robe one long straight piece of blue cloth with an opening in the centre for the head, and explains the bells by an eastern court custom: God appeared in the tabernacle as an emperor in his tent among his troops, and since at the doors of grandees a sonorous body was struck to advertise those within that a person sought admittance, the bells served that office for a tent that had a veil and no door. Wesley follows Henry on the robe and the bells and glosses the habergeon as a coat of armour.

Keil calls the robe a long closely fitting coat rather than a cloak, reaching only to the knees so as to show the coat beneath, against the Alexandrian rendering that makes it reach the feet; he identifies the habergeon of the reinforced neck-opening with the linen corselet such as Ajax wears in the Iliad, noting from Hengstenberg that Egypt made these in a highly artistic style, reports Rashi’s description of the pomegranates as round globes about the size of hens’ eggs, derives the word for bell from a root meaning to strike so that a bell and not a ball is meant, and cites the later explanation of the sound as a memorial with Hiskuni’s gloss that the people might know the hour of service and prepare their heart. Ellicott thinks the Hebrew word for habergeon Egyptian, but argues that the trimming is not: the pomegranate was an Assyrian favourite and not Egyptian, the bell more Assyrian still, its use in priestly costume without direct parallel and unknown in the religious services of any ancient nation, so that an entirely new religious usage seems to be introduced here. He makes the object of the bells corporate, publishing every movement of the people’s representative so that they might follow the service and offer a common worship.

debates: Whether the bells and pomegranates have any cultural precedent: Ellicott finds none and calls the usage entirely new, while Clarke supplies a parallel from eastern court practice.
How far the ornaments may be allegorised: Calvin builds a full figure on smell and sound and insists nothing in it is far-fetched, where Keil and Ellicott keep to the objects and their purpose.
outliers: Keil settles the shape of the bells lexically, from a root meaning to strike, ruling out the spherical ball some had supposed.

36.pericope_label: And thou shalt make a plate of pure gold, and grave upon it, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD; and it shall be upon Aaron’s forehead, that Aaron may bear the iniquity of the holy things, which the children of Israel shall hallow in all their holy gifts

schools.summary: Gill reports from Jarchi and Maimonides that the plate was two fingers broad and reached from ear to ear, which the Targum of Jonathan gives as from temple to temple, and calls it a priestly crown. Calvin explains its placing on the forehead as making it conspicuous, testifying both that the priesthood of God’s appointment is pleasing to him and that holiness is not to be sought elsewhere; on bearing the iniquity of the holy things he rules out any reference to gross sins, rejects as a poor exposition the view that mere ceremonial errors were remitted by the priest’s prayers, and insists that no offering, so far as it is of man, is free from guilt — our very holinesses need pardon, as water drawn pure from a fountain is made turbid passing over muddy ground — concluding that our best works convict us of guilt unless the holiness of Christ obtains pardon for them.

Clarke observes that the word rendered plate means a flower and that the Greek gives a leaf, and, since it is elsewhere called a crown and the author of Wisdom a diadem, proposes the radiated crown of the Roman emperors as its nearest shape, though worn round the forehead. He holds it allowed on all hands that the inscription stood in the primitive Hebrew character seen on ancient shekels, notes that its divine name is the word of four letters the Jews will neither write nor pronounce, and reports the Jewish tradition that the letters were embossed rather than cut and that the plate sat between the hair and the eyebrows. On the last clause he translates the verb as bearing in a vicarious and typical manner, observes that the same verb is used of the servant in Isaiah, and draws out the doubling, that Aaron atoned both for the people’s sins and for the imperfection of the atonement itself. Wesley presses the engraving as deep and durable rather than painted, and states that Christ bears this iniquity for us so as to bear it from us.

Keil derives the word for the plate from a root meaning to shine, notes that it is called the crown of holiness, and places it on a dark blue riband above the lower coil of the head-band, whose own name comes from a root meaning to twist and is used of no one but the high priest. Ellicott makes the plate the essence of the mitre, put forward first as that whereto all the rest is subordinate and catching the eye more than the breastplate, but only as the vehicle of an inscription teaching that religion culminates in holiness to the Lord, without which forms, ceremonies, attire, sacrifice and prayer are mockeries — a call to the whole nation and not the priest alone. He identifies the holy things as the people’s offerings, always imperfect through the imperfection of human nature and the mixed character of human motives, which the priest’s official holiness purged so that they could be presented without offence.

debates: What the plate’s form was: Clarke argues from the words for flower, leaf, crown and diadem toward a radiated band, while Keil derives the name from shining and describes only a flat plate on a riband.

How far the iniquity of the holy things extends: Calvin insists every human offering is guilty and rejects the narrower view that only ceremonial errors were covered, where Ellicott speaks of imperfection rather than guilt.
outliers: Clarke turns aside to palaeography, dating the inscription’s script to the character on ancient shekels and noting the Jewish refusal to write or pronounce the divine name it contained.

39.pericope_label: And thou shalt embroider the coat of fine linen, and thou shalt make the mitre of fine linen, and thou shalt make the girdle of needlework; and for Aaron’s sons thou shalt make coats, and girdles, and bonnets, for glory and for beauty; and thou shalt put them upon Aaron thy brother, and his sons with him, and shalt anoint them, and consecrate them

schools.summary: Gill canvasses three accounts of the tunic’s texture — full of eyelet holes, or holes like the sockets that held the stones so that gems were set into them (Jarchi), or figured with the small cornered cells of a ruminant’s stomach, network in form (Maimonides, approved by Braunius) — and prefers the last. On the vesting he treats the act itself as the investiture, since Moses put the garments on under God’s authority and from that point they had a right to exercise the office and might never officiate without them. Calvin explains the idiom of filling the hands: they are filled when the men are made fit to offer sacrifice, unconsecrated hands being accounted empty however full, since no gift is acceptable except in right of the priesthood. He stresses that Moses and not Aaron sanctifies them, so that the power rests in God and is not transferred to his ministers, suggests God was forestalling the charge that Aaron had made his own honour hereditary by fraud, and observes that Moses in inaugurating Aaron’s sons reduced his own to their proper place.

Henry notes that the inferior priests’ bonnets differed in shape from the high priest’s mitre, and turns the phrase for glory and for beauty against itself: all this glory was nothing compared with the glory of grace, and this beauty nothing to the beauty of holiness of which the garments were typical.

Wesley describes the tunic as reaching to the feet with sleeves to the wrists, bound to the body by a girdle of needlework, and takes the linen mitre to be such as kings anciently wore in the east, typifying the kingly office of Christ.

Ellicott marks the turn from outer garments to inner and disputes two renderings: embroider is generally agreed to be wrong (Kalisch reads weave, Gesenius work in chequer, Cook weave in diaper work) and coat is unfortunate for a long white tunic with tight sleeves reaching nearly to the feet, whose sleeves must have shown as the only covering of the arms. He notes that the girdle’s colours were needle-worked rather than woven and that little of it could be seen, and raises the difficulty that so plain a dress as the ordinary priests’ should suffice for glory and beauty, answering from the constant scriptural association of white robes with glory. Keil observes that the ordinary priests had the same articles but in plain cloth, their coat woven whole and without seam like the robe of Christ and reaching to the ankles, their head-dress named from a word for a cup and so shaped like an inverted cup; and he holds that because the dress was official, the reflected holiness of the office still left their sinful nature needing a special consecration.

debates: Whether the priests’ plain white dress can answer to for glory and for beauty: Ellicott raises the objection and answers from the symbolism of white robes, while Henry concedes the glory and subordinates it to holiness.
What the tunic’s peculiar weave was: Gill weighs eyelet holes, gem sockets and a reticulated network; Ellicott concludes only that the rare verb denotes some particular kind of weaving.
outliers: Calvin reads the consecration as a safeguard against future dynastic suspicion, arguing that Moses officiating protected Aaron from the charge of making the office hereditary and simultaneously excluded Moses’ own descendants.

42.pericope_label: And thou shalt make them linen breeches to cover their nakedness; from the loins even unto the thighs they shall reach: and they shall be upon Aaron, and upon his sons, when they come in unto the tabernacle of the congregation, that they bear not iniquity, and die: it shall be a statute for ever unto him and his seed after him

schools.summary: Gill takes the phrase as the flesh of nakedness, that part which when exposed causes shame and ridicule, and generalises that great care was taken in God’s house to preserve decency, prevent immodesty and guard against laughter and levity; he extends the requirement to all the garments and not the drawers only, and reports the Targum of Jonathan’s specification that the death would come by fire from heaven such as afterwards consumed Nadab and Abihu. Calvin states the principle behind so small a precept: men in their natural levity seize the slightest causes of offence to the disparagement of holy things, so God guards against it by requiring chaste and modest conduct lest anything indecorous impair the majesty of holy things. On the perpetual statute he objects that some improperly restrict it to the breeches when it covers the other ordinances too, and holds that its perpetuity attains its end in Christ, the figures being established precisely because their use ceased when their reality appeared, the priesthood being transferred and the law with it.

Clarke finds the command aimed outward at the shocking indecency of pagan worship, in which priests often ministered naked as in the sacrifices to Bacchus, and then states a rule for the whole chapter: the garments were doubtless emblematical, but of what and in what way no man can positively say, and where no clue guides us through a labyrinth in which mistake is possible at every moment it is better not to be wise above what is written, since reflections not clearly deducible from the text give little satisfaction to a sincere inquirer. He will allow four general senses only — purity in worship, the necessity of atonement, the purity and justice of the divine majesty, and the absolute necessity of holiness. Wesley states in a sentence that the statute continues as long as the priesthood and has its perpetuity in the substance of which these were shadows.

Keil explains that these verses stand apart because covering nakedness was an indispensable prerequisite rather than an ornament, derives the Hebrew name from a root meaning to conceal, and describes short drawers from hips to thighs; the material he leaves open, the word being uncertain, the parallel making it byssus or cotton yarn and the Greek rendering of linen no obstacle since the ancients used that word of fine white cotton too. He reads bearing iniquity and dying as incurring guilt deserving death, by disobedience or, more weightily, by violating the reverence due to God’s dwelling, and reasons that since the consciousness of sin first showed itself in the feeling of nakedness, those members are especially objects of shame. Ellicott corrects the English to drawers, notes that such drawers were the sole garment of many in Egypt and a necessary garment of all, identifies the holy place here with the court, and holds that the death threatened here and for neglecting the robe is probably a divine vengeance rather than a legal punishment.

debates: Whether the perpetual statute attaches to the breeches alone or to the whole priestly law: Calvin calls the narrow reading improper and extends it to the other ordinances.

How far the vestments may be interpreted symbolically: Clarke allows only four general senses and warns against being wise above what is written, where Calvin and Gill read particular garments typologically throughout.
outliers: Clarke uses the chapter’s least conspicuous item to lay down a general restraint on allegorical reading, effectively disowning much of the interpretation offered elsewhere in the catena.
